record.paper_title: Open questions on defining and computing the vapour-liquid surface tension by virial and test transformation approaches
record.original_question: For spherical vapour-liquid droplets and bubbles, how can one define, localize, or avoid the local virial or pressure tensor so that a surface tension computed from radial pressure profiles is unique, independent of the chosen scheme for assigning pair-interaction contributions to spatial locations, and has a direct thermodynamic interpretation? The difficulty is that a pair interaction between two molecules has no unique position in space: for planar interfaces the integral over the normal and tangential pressure profiles is unique even when the local profile is not, but for spherical interfaces the radial integral depends on the localization scheme.

evidence.quote: The local virial tensor (and pressure tensor) is always an underspecified quantity, but in the planar case, this does not matter because the volume integral over it yields a unique, well-defined result both for the overall pressure tensor and the surface tension. When integrating over the (virial as a function of the) radius in polar coordinates, this property disappears, and the surface tension is no longer well-defined.

When evaluating the virial and the pressure in a localized way, a non-uniqueness emerges from the way the potential energy of the system is given: As a sum over pairwise intermolecular interactions. Two interacting molecules i and j each have a well-defined position, but the interaction between them does not. Depending on how the virial from their interaction is distributed over the coordinate over which the profile is taken, results for the local pressure profile can differ.

For spherical interfaces, that is not the case. To begin with,there is no macromechanical expression that is independent of the scheme employed for localizing the contributions from each pairwise interaction.

For a spherical geometry, that is not the case. The result from integration over the profiles depends on the scheme for localizing the virial, and it does not have a direct thermodynamic interpretation.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a classical fluid of N point molecules in three-dimensional space interacting via pairwise potentials u(|r_i - r_j|), forming, in equilibrium, a spherically symmetric vapour-liquid configuration (a droplet or a bubble) centered at the origin. For a given localization scheme s, one assigns to each pair interaction (i,j) a continuous distribution along the segment (or other curve) connecting r_i and r_j; this defines a local virial tensor field and an associated local pressure tensor with normal component p_N^s(r) and tangential component p_T^s(r) depending only on the radial coordinate r = |r|.

For a planar interface (flat geometry), the integrals
  ∫ [p_N(z) - p_T(z)] dz   and   ∫ p_N(z) dz,   ∫ p_T(z) dz
taken over the direction normal to the interface are independent of the localization scheme s, although the local profiles themselves are not. In particular, the surface tension γ obtained as the integral of p_N - p_T across the interface is uniquely defined and admits a direct thermodynamic interpretation.

For a spherically symmetric interface, the analogous radial integral
  γ_s(R) = ∫_0^∞ f(r, R) [p_N^s(r) - p_T^s(r)] dr
(for any standard choice of dividing surface R and weight f, e.g. as in the Irving–Kirkwood or Harasima conventions) does depend on the localization scheme s, and there is no known macromechanical expression for the surface tension of a spherical interface that is independent of s and admits a direct thermodynamic interpretation.

Problem. Provide a definition or procedure that, for spherical vapour-liquid droplets and bubbles in a system with pairwise interactions, either (a) localizes the virial / pressure tensor in such a way that the resulting surface tension obtained from radial pressure profiles is unique (independent of the scheme used to assign pair-interaction contributions to spatial locations) and has a direct thermodynamic interpretation, or (b) avoids the local pressure tensor altogether while yielding a surface tension with these two properties (uniqueness and direct thermodynamic interpretation). Alternatively, prove that no such definition exists.
artifact.status_search_result: The non-uniqueness of the local pressure tensor for curved (spherical) interfaces is a long-standing issue going back to Irving–Kirkwood and Harasima, and remains an active area of debate. Recent work (2023–2025) continues to propose alternative routes (test-area, virial-route, mechanical vs. thermodynamic definitions) without arriving at a universally accepted unique scheme-independent surface tension for spherical interfaces. No definitive resolution appears in the literature.
